messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 37
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Financial Analyst
- Trauma Type: Captivity
- Pcl5: 59

# Marcus

Marcus sits with his back against the wall in the therapy office, a habit he's developed without quite realizing it. At thirty-seven, he has the lean, watchful quality of someone who has learned to minimize his presence. He works as a financial analyst for a mid-sized investment firm, a job that requires precision and forward-thinking—skills that feel increasingly at odds with how his mind actually functions these days.

Five years ago, Marcus was on a hiking trip in Eastern Europe when he was taken. He and two companions were separated from their group, and within hours, he found himself in a remote location with three men who demanded money. What began as a negotiation became a nightmare. The other hikers were released after ransoms were paid, but Marcus remained. For forty-three days, he was held in a basement room with minimal light, inconsistent food, and the constant threat of violence. His captors seemed almost indifferent to him—he was simply leverage in a larger operation. The psychological weight of that indifference, he later realizes, was sometimes worse than direct aggression.

He was eventually freed during a police raid, physically intact but fundamentally altered.

In the years since, Marcus has functioned on the surface. He returned to work after six months, divorced his wife—who couldn't understand why he seemed like a stranger—and maintained his apartment and his professional responsibilities. But underneath, he exists in a state of persistent vigilance. At work, he positions his desk so he can see the office entrance. He arrives early and leaves late, uncomfortable in the communal spaces where he might be trapped. During market analysis meetings, his mind sometimes fractures; he'll be discussing stock portfolios and suddenly become aware that he's calculating exits, counting people, assessing threats.

Sleep has become something he negotiates with rather than experiences. He lies awake for hours, his mind cycling through the same memories—the sound of the basement door opening, the unpredictability of when his captors would appear, the particular quality of darkness in that room. When he does sleep, he often wakes gasping, convinced he's back there, his heart racing as though his body hasn't yet received the message that he's safe. His apartment is well-lit at night. He sleeps with his bedroom door unlocked, counterintuitively, because the idea of being trapped behind a locked door feels worse than any external threat.

Loud noises trigger something visceral in him. A car backfiring, a door slamming—these ordinary sounds send electricity through his nervous system. His colleagues have noticed his startle response, though he's become adept at covering it. Last month, a coworker came up behind him to discuss a report, and Marcus nearly knocked him down, his body moving before his mind caught up.

He avoids situations where he might feel confined. He takes the stairs instead of elevators, even in his office building. He hasn't been on public transportation in three years. He declines social invitations, particularly anything involving groups or unfamiliar locations. The divorce wasn't really about his ex-wife; it was about the fact that sleeping next to another person felt impossible, that her presence in his space triggered an anxiety he couldn't explain to her.

Marcus intellectually understands that he's safe now. He can analyze probability and risk with the same precision he applies to financial data. The logical part of his brain knows that the chances of this happening again are infinitesimal. But his body has learned a different calculus, one based on the forty-three days when the world proved itself fundamentally unpredictable and dangerous. That knowledge lives in his nervous system now, in the way his muscles tense at unexpected sounds, in the constant low-level surveillance he maintains of his environment.

He tells his therapist he wants to feel normal again, though he's no longer entirely sure what that means.
